title: Slip stitch
subtitle: The flattest stitch, used to join and to travel
excerpt: The slip stitch is the shortest stitch in crochet, barely taller than a chain. It adds almost no height, which makes it the stitch of choice for joining a round into a ring, moving the hook across without building fabric, and seaming pieces together.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passage Dillmont titles the single stitch (Fig. 404), which is the modern slip stitch. Public domain via Project Gutenberg. The slip stitch carries the same name in UK and US terminology.

glossaryTerms.definition: The shortest crochet stitch, made by pulling the yarn straight through both the stitch and the loop on the hook in one move. It adds almost no height, so it is used to join, to travel across stitches, and to seam.
Closing a worked round into a ring by working a slip stitch into the first stitch of that round, so the round becomes continuous.
The single live loop on the hook between stitches. Every stitch starts and ends with one working loop.

content.text: is the shortest stitch in crochet, barely taller than a chain. It adds almost no height, so its job is rarely to build fabric. Instead it joins, it travels, and it seams. Dillmont called this the single stitch in 1886; the modern name is slip stitch in both British and American patterns.

content.text: Insert the hook into the next stitch or chain space.
Wrap the yarn over the hook once.
Draw the yarn through the stitch and through the loop on the hook in one smooth pull. One loop is left, and the slip stitch is made.
Keep slip stitches loose. They tend to tighten, and a tight row of them is hard to work into afterwards.

into a ring at the end of each round of a motif. Worked along the tops of stitches, slip stitches carry the hook across to a new starting point without adding a row. Worked through both edges of two pieces held together, they make a firm, flat seam. A surface line of slip stitches can also be used as a decorative ridge on top of finished fabric.

Worked into the back loops only, rows of slip stitches make a stretchy ribbing for cuffs and hat brims. An invisible join finishes the last round of a motif by mimicking the top of a stitch instead of using a plain slip stitch, for a tidier seam in the round. The whipstitch and the slip-stitch seam are the two usual ways to join motifs, and the slip stitch underpins both.
Difficulty: beginner. The motion is simple; the only knack is keeping it loose enough to work into later.
